events.excerpt: Two email addresses used to send bomb threats that disrupted thousands of Italian schools this week were found exposed in infostealer logs for over a year, experts say. Researchers at Hudson Rock looked into the two university email addresses used to send the bomb threats. One, from Egypt’s Kafrelsheikh University, was scooped up by Vidar – a cybercrime tool that steals saved account credentials and passwords from an infected computer and leaks them to attackers – as far back as October 2021. The other, from Taiwan's Dayeh University, was found among the 284 million addresses included in the massive AlienTXTBASE infostealer dump , dated February 2025. The experts said that the two addresses in infostealer logs do not strictly mean that those behind the bomb threats gained access to the accounts using the previous infostealer compromise. However, it suggests that there was ample time for the universities and Microsoft, which both universities used for authentication, to take action against the accounts that they should have been aware were appearing in infostealer logs. Modern threat intelligence has made infostealer logs highly visible. "Both findings place credential exposure well before the disruption, creating a substantial window in which exposed access could have been invest
events.headline: Email addresses used in European school bomb hoaxes spotted in old infostealer logs

events.excerpt: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates. Read full article Comments
events.headline: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights

events.excerpt: Your tongue might not seem like the most obvious way to control a computer, but it's actually well suited to the job. It's fast, precise, and capable of reaching individual teeth without any visual guidance. Researchers at Aarhus University have taken advantage of these abilities to develop TeethMark , a wearable interface that lets users control electronic devices by touching their teeth with their tongue. The device resembles a transparent dental retainer that fits over the teeth. Embedded in the custom-made brace is a flexible printed circuit board containing electrodes that detect tongue movements through capacitive sensing. The system recognizes three types of gestures: tapping individual teeth, sliding the tongue across multiple teeth, and touching several teeth simultaneously. Unlike standard touch interfaces, TeethMark also provides electrotactile feedback. Electrodes on the inner surfaces of the teeth deliver small electrical pulses that users can feel with their tongues. Additional electrodes on the outer surfaces stimulate the inside of the lips, allowing notifications to be delivered without requiring any tongue movement. The hardware is built around an ESP32 microcontroller, which handles capacitive sensing and controls the electrical stimulation circuitry. A MOSFET
events.headline: TeethMark Puts a Computer Interface in Your Mouth

events.excerpt: As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday's global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It's not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point. It's not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus —one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. Even then, while growth occurs exponentially for a time, it does not continue forever. events.excerpt: It’s the second Tuesday of the month, and that means another Microsoft Patch Tuesday. The new normal is that the numbers are hard to believe. Brian Krebs reports that this month’s release fixes nearly 1,100 vulnerabilities, 63 of them rated critical, and over 500 that let an attacker elevate their privileges. Only one is reported as actively exploited: CVE-2026-124194 , a spoofing bug in Outlook. Microsoft has now shipped more than 5,100 security fixes this year, after more than 1,400 last month, compared to an average of around 100 a month last year. Obviously AI tools get the credit for the volume of bugs fixed, but also of course for the volume of bugs found. Everyone else is busy too. Apple pushed out-of-cycle updates for at least nine vulnerabilities across its operating systems, including an iMessage flaw which could let a remote attacker join a group chat and read its messages, and backported the fixes to iOS 18. Chrome 157 fixes CVE-2026-125350 , another Chrome zero-day, a week after a Chrome release which fixed more than 200 bugs, Firefox 160 fixes almost 100 CVEs, and Adobe fixed more than 110. Also since last week, zlib 1.4 shipped with more than a dozen security fixes, eight more vulnerabilities were disclosed in the X.Org server and XWayland, and Microsoft’s own Azur
events.headline: This Week In Security: Four-Digit Patch Tuesday, SSH Exploited, GitBook Breach, Android GhostMap
